q: According to Newton's second law, an object that is accelerating must have a net force acting on it.
e: True. According to Newton's second law, an object that is accelerating must have a net force acting on it. Newton's second law says a net force is required whenever there is acceleration, F_net = ma.

q: According to Newton's second law, an object that is accelerating must have a net torque acting on it.
e: False. Newton's second law for linear acceleration uses net force, F_net = ma, not net torque. The error is the part about According Newton second law object accelerating.

q: An object moving in a circle must have a force applied to it to keep it moving in the circle.
e: True. An object moving in a circle must have a force applied to it to keep it moving in the circle. Newton's second law needs a net inward force F_c = m a_C whenever the path is a circle.

q: An object moving in a straight line must have a centripetal force applied to it to keep it moving.
e: False. Centripetal force is for circular paths, not straight-line motion. A straight-line path does not need a centre-seeking force.

q: The force applied to an object to keep it moving in a circle is known as the centripetal force.
e: True. The force applied to an object to keep it moving in a circle is known as the centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: The force applied to an object to keep it moving in a circle is known as the centrifugal force.
e: False. The inward force that keeps circular motion is centripetal force, not centrifugal force. The error is the part about force applied object keep moving circle.

q: For uniform circular motion, the acceleration is centripetal acceleration which is directed towards the centre of the circle at any moment.
e: True. For uniform circular motion, the acceleration is centripetal acceleration which is directed towards the centre of the circle at any moment. In uniform circular motion the speed is constant, but velocity still changes direction so a_C is present.

q: For uniform circular motion, the acceleration is centripetal acceleration which is directed away from the centre of the circle at any moment.
e: False. Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre. a_C is inward, toward the centre, not outward.

q: In the absence of centripetal force, the object would not move along a circle but move in a straight line, according to Newton's first law.
e: True. In the absence of centripetal force, the object would not move along a circle but move in a straight line, according to Newton's first law. A straight-line path does not need a centre-seeking force.

q: In the absence of centripetal force, the object would continue moving along a circle, according to Newton's first law.
e: False. Without centripetal force, Newton's first law sends the object off in a straight line. The error is the part about absence centripetal force object continue moving.

q: Using Newton's second law, the magnitude of the centripetal force is $F_c = m a_c$.
e: True. Using Newton's second law, the magnitude of the centripetal force is F_c = m a_c. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: Using Newton's second law, the magnitude of the centripetal force is $F_c = \frac{m}{a_c}$.
e: False. Newton's second law gives F_c = m a_c, not m/a_c. The error is the part about Newton second law magnitude centripetal force.

q: Substituting $v = r\omega$ in the centripetal force equation gives $F_c = m r \omega^2$.
e: True. Substituting v = rω in the centripetal force equation gives F_c = m r ω². Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: Substituting $v = r\omega$ in the centripetal force equation gives $F_c = m r^2 \omega$.
e: False. Substituting v = rω yields F_c = m r ω², not m r² ω. The error is the part about Substituting centripetal force equation gives.

q: To swing a ball on the end of a string in a circle, the tension in the string provides the required centripetal force.
e: True. To swing a ball on the end of a string in a circle, the tension in the string provides the required centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: To swing a ball on the end of a string in a horizontal circle, the weight of the ball provides the required centripetal force.
e: False. In a horizontal whirl the string tension provides centripetal force, not the ball's weight. The error is the part about swing ball end string horizontal circle.

q: The gravitational force of the earth on the moon orbiting the earth is an example of a centripetal force.
e: True. The gravitational force of the earth on the moon orbiting the earth is an example of a centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: The gravitational force of the earth on the moon orbiting the earth is an example of a centrifugal force.
e: False. Earth's gravity on the Moon is the centripetal force of the orbit, not a centrifugal force. The error is the part about gravitational force earth moon orbiting example.

q: The electric force acting on an electron orbiting the nucleus acts as the required centripetal force.
e: True. The electric force acting on an electron orbiting the nucleus acts as the required centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: The magnetic force acting on an electron orbiting the nucleus acts as the required centripetal force.
e: False. The inward force on an orbiting electron is the electrostatic Coulomb force, not a magnetic force. The error is the part about magnetic force acting electron orbiting nucleus.

q: When whirling a body attached to a string, if the tension force is normal to the direction of motion, it causes the body to move in a circular path.
e: True. When whirling a body attached to a string, if the tension force is normal to the direction of motion, it causes the body to move in a circular path. Inward tension is perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes direction without doing speed work.

q: When whirling a body attached to a string, if the tension force is parallel to the direction of motion, it causes the body to move in a circular path.
e: False. Tension must point toward the centre, perpendicular to the velocity, to keep circular motion. The error is the part about whirling body attached string tension force.

q: An attractive gravitational force exists between the sun and the earth in a direction perpendicular to the path of the earth.
e: True. An attractive gravitational force exists between the sun and the earth in a direction perpendicular to the path of the earth. Sun-Earth gravity is radial, at right angles to the instantaneous orbital velocity.

q: An attractive gravitational force exists between the sun and the earth in a direction parallel to the path of the earth.
e: False. Sun-Earth gravity is radial, toward the Sun, not parallel to Earth's orbital path. The error is the part about attractive gravitational force exists sun earth.

q: The Coulomb attractive force between the nucleus and the electron acts as the required centripetal force.
e: True. The Coulomb attractive force between the nucleus and the electron acts as the required centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: The Coulomb repulsive force between the nucleus and the electron acts as the required centripetal force.
e: False. The nucleus-electron force is Coulomb attraction, and that attraction supplies the centripetal force. The error is the part about Coulomb repulsive force nucleus electron acts.

q: When a car turns in a circular path, a frictional force exists between the road and the car tires, acting normally to the direction of motion.
e: True. When a car turns in a circular path, a frictional force exists between the road and the car tires, acting normally to the direction of motion. On a level curve, static friction points toward the centre, normal to the car's heading.

q: When a car turns in a circular path, a frictional force exists between the road and the car tires, acting parallel to the direction of motion.
e: False. Tension must point toward the centre, perpendicular to the velocity, to keep circular motion. The error is the part about car turns circular path frictional force.

q: When a car moves in a circular path which is inclined to the horizontal, the horizontal component of the normal force provides the required centripetal force.
e: True. When a car moves in a circular path which is inclined to the horizontal, the horizontal component of the normal force provides the required centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: When a car moves in a circular path which is inclined to the horizontal, the vertical component of the normal force provides the required centripetal force.
e: False. On a banked curve the horizontal component of the normal force supplies centripetal requirement, not the vertical component. The error is the part about car moves circular path inclined horizontal.

q: The upward thrust (lifting force) on an aeroplane acts normally to the aeroplane body.
e: True. The upward thrust (lifting force) on an aeroplane acts normally to the aeroplane body. Lift is perpendicular to the wing/body, so banking gives that lift a horizontal centripetal part.

q: The upward thrust (lifting force) on an aeroplane acts parallel to the aeroplane body.
e: False. Lift on a wing is normal to the wing, not parallel to the fuselage. The error is the part about upward thrust lifting force aeroplane acts.

q: When an aeroplane tilts, the horizontal component of the lifting force provides the centripetal force.
e: True. When an aeroplane tilts, the horizontal component of the lifting force provides the centripetal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: When an aeroplane tilts, the vertical component of the lifting force provides the centripetal force.
e: False. When an aeroplane banks, the horizontal component of lift supplies centripetal force, not the vertical component. The error is the part about aeroplane tilts vertical component lifting force.

q: On a flat unbanked road, the centripetal force for an automobile driving round a curve is supplied by friction between the tires and the road.
e: True. On a flat unbanked road, the centripetal force for an automobile driving round a curve is supplied by friction between the tires and the road. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: On a flat unbanked road, the centripetal force for an automobile driving round a curve is supplied by the normal force.
e: False. On a flat unbanked road, friction of the tires supplies the centripetal force, not the vertical normal force. The error is the part about flat unbanked road centripetal force automobile.

q: If the frictional force is not sufficient on an unbanked road, the car will skid out of the circular path.
e: True. If the frictional force is not sufficient on an unbanked road, the car will skid out of the circular path. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: If the normal force is not sufficient on an unbanked road, the car will skid out of the circular path.
e: False. On a flat unbanked road, friction of the tires supplies the centripetal force, not the vertical normal force. The error is the part about normal force sufficient unbanked road car.

q: Banking of roads is raising the outer edge of the curved road higher than the inner edge.
e: True. Banking of roads is raising the outer edge of the curved road higher than the inner edge. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: Banking of roads is raising the inner edge of the curved road higher than the outer edge.
e: False. Particles at every radius move in circles about the axis, not just the outer edge. The error is the part about Banking roads raising inner edge curved.

q: The angle that the inclined track makes with the horizontal is called the angle of banking.
e: True. The angle that the inclined track makes with the horizontal is called the angle of banking. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: The angle that the inclined track makes with the vertical is called the angle of banking.
e: False. Angle of banking is the tilt of the track to the horizontal, not to the vertical. The error is the part about angle inclined track makes vertical banking.

q: The normal force exerted by a banked road is perpendicular to the road.
e: True. The normal force exerted by a banked road is perpendicular to the road. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: The normal force exerted by a banked road is parallel to the road.
e: False. The normal force is perpendicular to the road surface, not parallel to it. The error is the part about normal force exerted banked road parallel.

q: For every banked curve, there is a limiting speed at which the entire centripetal force is supplied by the horizontal component of the normal force.
e: True. For every banked curve, there is a limiting speed at which the entire centripetal force is supplied by the horizontal component of the normal force. Centripetal force is the real net inward force that keeps an object on a circular path, F_c = mv²/r.

q: For every banked curve, there is a limiting speed at which the entire centripetal force is supplied by the vertical component of the normal force.
e: False. At the design speed the horizontal component of N supplies the whole centripetal force. The error is the part about every banked curve limiting speed entire.

q: At the limiting speed on a banked curve, the frictional force between the tires and the road is not required.
e: True. At the limiting speed on a banked curve, the frictional force between the tires and the road is not required. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: At the limiting speed on a banked curve, the frictional force between the tires and the road is at its maximum value.
e: False. At the design (limiting) banked speed, friction can be zero; N's horizontal part does the job. The error is the part about limiting speed banked curve frictional force.

q: According to the banking angle equation, $\tan \theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$.
e: True. According to the banking angle equation, tan θ = (v²)/(rg). A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: According to the banking angle equation, $\sin \theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}$.
e: False. The banking relation is tanθ = v²/(rg), not sinθ = v²/(rg). The error is the part about According banking angle equation sin.

q: In the banking of roads, since there is no vertical motion, the net force on the car in the y direction is zero.
e: True. In the banking of roads, since there is no vertical motion, the net force on the car in the y direction is zero. A banked track tilts so the horizontal part of the normal force can supply some or all of the centripetal requirement.

q: In the banking of roads, since there is no vertical motion, the net force on the car in the y direction is equal to the centripetal force.
e: False. Vertical net force is zero if there is no vertical acceleration. Centripetal force is the horizontal net force.
